text: In 1861, Chicago lifted a giant brick hotel into the air.
With the guests still inside.
Chicago was built on a swamp.
The streets were rivers of mud, and the sewage had nowhere to go.
Diseases like cholera kept breaking out.
So the city made a wild decision.
Raise the whole city several feet, and build the sewers underneath.
The streets were easy.
But the buildings had to go up too.
The biggest one was the Tremont House, a huge brick hotel.
A young engineer named George Pullman and his partners took the job.
They put about five thousand jackscrews under the building, and hired hundreds of men.
On a signal, every man gave his screws a tiny turn.
Then another.
And another.
Inch by inch, the hotel rose six feet.
And the hotel never closed.
Guests kept eating, sleeping, and checking in, while the building rose beneath them.
Reportedly, not a single window broke.
Pullman later got rich building railway sleeping cars.
So people could sleep, while the world moved beneath them.
